query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy provides a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor integrity and tends to crack. Prior studies on related MM′X materials used epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe, obtaining compressive strengths of 152 and 218 MPa at two epoxy contents, and low-melting In composites, obtaining 48 MPa compressive strength and more than eight times the thermal conductivity of epoxy-containing samples under the reported conditions. These routes demonstrated gains in selected strength or heat-transport metrics, but the desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved. The target should also remain rare-earth-free. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing caloric response? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, quantitative or directional outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, boundary conditions under applied-field, pressure, temperature, and loading regimes, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive controlled experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloys with varying amounts of Cr, and test their mechanical properties, such as compressive strength and ductility, under applied-field and pressure-field operation, as well as their caloric response.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the introduction of Cr does not lead to improved integrity, or if the caloric response is significantly sacrificed, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractInvestigation into non-equiatomic high-entropy alloys has grown in recent years due to questions about the role of entropy stabilization in forming single-phase solid solutions. Non-equiatomic alloys have been shown to retain the outstanding mechanical properties exhibited by their equiatomic counterparts and even improve electrical, thermal, and magnetic properties, albeit with relaxed composition bounds. However, much remains to understand the processing–structure–property relationships in all classes of so-called high-entropy alloys (HEAs). Here, we are motivated by the natural phenomena of crystal growth and equilibrium conditions to introduce a method of HEA development where controlled processing conditions determine the most probable and stable composition. This is demonstrated by cooling an equiatomic CrMnFeCoNiCu alloy from the melt steadily over 3 days (cooling rate ~4 °C/h). The result is an alloy containing large Cr-rich precipitates and an almost Cr-free matrix exhibiting compositions within the MnFeCoNiCu system (with trace amounts of Cr). AbstractHigh-entropy alloys have gained widespread concern in response to the increased requirements for future high-temperature structural superalloys. By combining phase-diagram calculations with microhardness, compression behavior measurements at room temperature, and elevated temperature conditions, the very important role of the Cr element on the microstructure and properties is deeply revealed, which provides candidates materials for future high-temperature alloy applications. The increment of Cr favors the regulation of the two-phase fraction and distribution. The thermodynamic calculations illustrate that the density and melting point of the HEAs showed an increasing trend with the increase of the Cr content. The typical worm-like microstructure of the Cr0.6 alloy with a dual BCC structure was detected. Meanwhile, on the one hand, the increment of the Cr elements results in a considerable optimization of the mechanical properties of the alloy in terms of strength and ductility at room temperature. Developing lightweight alloys with excellent strength and ductility is always the objective for the application of structural alloys due to the demand for high-performance superalloys in increased harsh working conditions. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) and multiprincipal element alloys have received considerable interest for community experts and have become a worldwide hot spot since Cantor and Yeh reported their first publication [,]. Cr-containing HEAs have exhibited promising potential when applied in high-temperature industrial fields as a result of their remarkable strength [,,,], favorable ductility [,,], distinguished corrosion resistance [,,], superior wear and oxidation resistance [,,], and acceptable thermal stability [,]. So far, great endeavors have been devoted to examining the properties of Cr-containing HEAs with the incorporation of the Cr element, not limited to the investigations of corrosion behavior, high-temperature oxidation behavior, and thermal stability of the HEAs, especially regarding the evolution of the microstructure and mechanical behavior with different Cr content, is still a top research priority. decision.trend: Research on high-entropy alloys has focused on improving their mechanical properties, such as strength and ductility, while maintaining their unique characteristics, such as high entropy and random distribution of elements. Recent studies have explored the effects of processing conditions, microstructure, and composition on the properties of high-entropy alloys. The trend suggests that optimizing the composition, microstructure, and processing conditions can lead to improved mechanical properties and potentially overcome the limitations of high-entropy alloys, such as poor integrity and tendency to crack.
decision.unsolved: The poor integrity and tendency to crack of the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy remain unsolved, despite efforts to improve its mechanical properties through various approaches, such as epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe and low-melting In composites. The desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved.
decision.why: Optimizing the composition of the high-entropy alloy could lead to improved mechanical properties, such as strength and ductility, while maintaining its unique characteristics. This approach has been explored in recent studies, which have demonstrated the potential for improved properties through composition optimization. By optimizing the composition, it may be possible to overcome the limitations of the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy and achieve the desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance.
